fig_function_bar.png.title: Which financing functions are studied most?
fig_function_bar.png.caption: Benefits decisions and purchasing have the most studies. A study may cover several financing functions.

fig_function_second_opinion_v2_2.png.title: How an extra classification check changes the results
fig_function_second_opinion_v2_2.png.caption: Adding labels from the extra classification check changes each function’s share only slightly.

fig_outcome_lollipop.png.title: What do the studies measure?
fig_outcome_lollipop.png.caption: “Other” includes identifiable outcomes outside the eight named groups. A study may examine several outcomes.

fig_function_outcome_heatmap.png.title: Which outcomes are studied for each financing function?
fig_function_outcome_heatmap.png.caption: Each row shows the outcomes examined by studies covering that financing function. Darker cells mean a larger share; shares can exceed 100%.

fig_function_time_lines.png.title: How the financing functions studied have changed over time
fig_function_time_lines.png.caption: Benefits decisions accounted for 27% of eligible studies at the start of the period and 25% at the end. A study may cover several functions.

fig_method_stream.png.title: How research on each financing function has grown
fig_method_stream.png.caption: Financing-function assignments grew 1.9 times between 2010 and 2025. This counts functions assigned to studies, rather than unique studies.

fig_alluvial.png.title: How study methods, financing functions and outcomes overlap
fig_alluvial.png.caption: Wider bands represent more studies. Each study is shown with one financing function and one outcome, selected from its recorded labels.

fig_outcome_other_themes_v5.png.title: What is included in “Other” outcomes?
fig_outcome_other_themes_v5.png.caption: Service use, access and coverage, and spending, prices and funding are the largest groups within “Other”.
fig_outcome_other_themes_v5.png.warning: 6,830 studies classified as Other could not be assigned a theme and are not shown. A study may appear in several themes.

fig_outcome_trend_v5.png.title: How the outcomes studied have changed over time
fig_outcome_trend_v5.png.caption: The share examining health improvement rose from 8% to 13%; financial protection rose from 7% to 9%, between 2010 and 2025.

fig_theme_rank.png.title: The 20 largest groups of research topics
fig_theme_rank.png.caption: The largest groups concern insurance programmes and medicines. Labels show characteristic words from each group.

fig_topicmap.png.title: Groups of studies with similar topics
fig_topicmap.png.caption: Each dot represents a study; nearby dots have more similar abstracts. This is a map of topics, not a geographic map.
fig_topicmap.png.warning: Earlier dataset: these two maps use the September 2026 set of 36,495 studies, not the current 53,411-study map.

fig_topicmap_income.png.title: Which topic groups focus on lower-income countries?
fig_topicmap_income.png.caption: Colours show how often each topic group’s single-country studies examine low- and middle-income countries.
fig_topicmap_income.png.warning: Earlier dataset: these two maps use the September 2026 set of 36,495 studies, not the current 53,411-study map.

fig_topic_landscape.png.title: Which research fields do the studies belong to?
fig_topic_landscape.png.caption: Longer bars represent more studies in each research field. The fields come from publication metadata.

fig_topic_landscape_treemap.png.title: Which research fields have the most studies?
fig_topic_landscape_treemap.png.caption: Larger boxes represent more studies. Economics and Econometrics is the largest research field among studies with a field label.

fig_disease_circular.png.title: Which disease areas are studied?
fig_disease_circular.png.caption: The figures cover studies assigned a disease category, rather than all studies in the map. Bar length shows the share in each disease area.
fig_disease_circular.png.warning: Disease classifications are available for 7,881 of the 53,411 studies, so these figures describe a subset.

fig_disease_method.png.title: Which financing functions are studied in each disease area?
fig_disease_method.png.caption: Each row shows the financing functions covered by studies in that disease area. A study may cover several functions, so shares can exceed 100%.
fig_disease_method.png.warning: Disease classifications are available for 7,881 of the 53,411 studies, so these figures describe a subset.

fig_funder_opportunity.png.title: Which financing functions receive more attention in each disease area?
fig_funder_opportunity.png.caption: Red cells show financing functions that are more common in a disease area than across disease-classified studies; blue cells show functions that are less common.
fig_funder_opportunity.png.warning: Disease classifications are available for 7,881 of the 53,411 studies, so these figures describe a subset.

fig_transition.png.title: How the disease areas studied in lower-income countries have changed
fig_transition.png.caption: Among disease-classified studies about low- and middle-income countries, non-communicable diseases became a larger share of research between 2010 and 2025.
fig_transition.png.warning: Disease classifications are available for 7,881 of the 53,411 studies, so these figures describe a subset.

fig_funder_trajectory.png.title: How research about lower-income countries has changed by disease area
fig_funder_trajectory.png.caption: Dots show 2010–2017 and arrowheads show 2018–2026. An arrow to the right means a larger share of that disease area’s research concerns low- and middle-income countries.
fig_funder_trajectory.png.warning: Disease classifications are available for 7,881 of the 53,411 studies, so these figures describe a subset.

fig_map_disease.png.title: Where each disease area has been studied
fig_map_disease.png.caption: The maps show where studies in each disease area were identified. Darker colours mean more studies.
fig_map_disease.png.warning: Disease classifications are available for 7,881 of the 53,411 studies, so these figures describe a subset.

fig_methods_characteristics.png.title: How the studies were carried out
fig_methods_characteristics.png.caption: Cross-sectional and correlational studies are the most common design. Routine administrative records are the most common data source. Study-design labels mix research methods with the focus of the study, and each study has only one.

fig_worldmap.png.title: Which countries the studies examine
fig_worldmap.png.caption: The map shows studies examining each country, per 10 million people. A study counts in every country it covers.

fig_top_countries.png.title: The 20 most-studied countries
fig_top_countries.png.caption: The United States is the country most often studied. A study covering several countries counts in each.

fig_income_bar.png.title: Study–country pairs by income group of the country examined
fig_income_bar.png.caption: Each bar counts study–country pairs: a study examining three countries counts three times, once per country.

fig_map_growth.png.title: Which countries have more recent research?
fig_map_growth.png.caption: Colour shows the share of a country’s studies published in 2018–2026. A higher share means more recent research, rather than necessarily faster growth.

fig_map_method.png.title: The most common analysis approach in studies examining each country
fig_map_method.png.caption: Colour shows the most common analysis approach among studies examining each country. Countries examined by fewer than five studies are not classified.

fig_glance_regions.html.title: Research coverage relative to health spending
fig_glance_regions.html.caption: Compare studies relative to health spending and explore the regional profiles. A high number of studies per dollar can reflect low spending, rather than a large research base.

fig_map_bivariate.png.title: Countries with high disease burden and little research in this map
fig_map_bivariate.png.caption: The colours combine low, middle and high levels of disease burden and study counts. Red identifies countries with high burden and relatively few studies in this map.

fig_map_burden.png.title: Research relative to disease burden, by country
fig_map_burden.png.caption: The map shows studies per 100,000 healthy years lost through illness or early death. Red indicates more research relative to burden; blue indicates less.

fig_map_deserts.png.title: Countries with no studies identified in this map
fig_map_deserts.png.caption: Djibouti has disease-burden data but no included study naming it. This does not establish that no research exists there.

fig_burden.png.title: How research coverage compares with disease burden
fig_burden.png.caption: The middle-ranked high-income country has 15 times as many studies per unit of disease burden as the middle-ranked low-income country.

fig_deficit.png.title: How study counts compare with a disease-burden benchmark
fig_deficit.png.caption: This comparison asks what study counts would look like if countries’ research shares matched their shares of disease burden. It is an illustrative benchmark.

fig_injustice.png.title: Research share compared with disease-burden share
fig_injustice.png.caption: Countries below the comparison line have a smaller share of studies than their share of disease burden. This is a benchmark, rather than a recommended research allocation.

fig_equity_time.png.title: How the share of research about lower-income countries has changed
fig_equity_time.png.caption: The share of single-country studies about low- and middle-income countries rose from 25% in 2010 to 41% in 2025.

fig_inequality.png.title: How research is concentrated across lower-income countries
fig_inequality.png.caption: Research is unevenly distributed across low- and middle-income countries. The five most-studied countries account for 46% of their evidence base.

fig_forest.png.title: How research approaches and local authorship differ by income group
fig_forest.png.caption: Research approach and the inclusion of locally based authors differ by country income group. These adjusted associations do not show cause and effect.
fig_forest.png.warning: The chart shows adjusted odds ratios, not probability ratios. Associations do not establish cause and effect.

fig_map_authorship.png.title: How often do studies include an author based in the country studied?
fig_map_authorship.png.caption: The map shows how often studies include at least one author based in the country studied. Author location refers to institutional affiliation, not nationality or leadership.
fig_map_authorship.png.warning: Author locations are available for only part of the evidence base and do not establish who led the research.

fig_authorship_pattern.png.title: Where are authors of research about each income group based?
fig_authorship_pattern.png.caption: Among studies about low-income countries with author-location information, 18% have only locally based authors, 50% have mixed teams and 32% have no locally based author.
fig_authorship_pattern.png.warning: Author locations are available for only part of the evidence base and do not establish who led the research.

fig_authorship_by_function.png.title: Local authorship by health financing function
fig_authorship_by_function.png.caption: The share including a locally based author ranges from 84% for the Overall category to 95% for Purchasing. These shares do not identify research leaders.
fig_authorship_by_function.png.warning: Author locations are available for only part of the evidence base and do not establish who led the research.

fig_authorship_outcome_heatmap.png.title: Author-team locations by outcome studied
fig_authorship_outcome_heatmap.png.caption: Each row shows where authors are based for studies examining that outcome. Mixed teams include authors based both inside and outside the country studied.
fig_authorship_outcome_heatmap.png.warning: Author locations are available for only part of the evidence base and do not establish who led the research.

fig_collab_chord.png.title: Collaboration between authors in different income groups
fig_collab_chord.png.caption: Bands link income groups whose authors collaborate on the same studies. Wider bands mean more studies; within-group studies are excluded from the bands.
fig_collab_chord.png.warning: Author locations are available for only part of the evidence base and do not establish who led the research.

fig_funder_capacity.png.title: Where studies include fewer authors based locally
fig_funder_capacity.png.caption: Countries differ in the share of studies that include a locally based author. This measure alone does not establish local research capacity.
fig_funder_capacity.png.warning: Author locations are available for only part of the evidence base and do not establish who led the research.

fig_funder_types_v5.png.title: Which types of organisations fund the research?
fig_funder_types_v5.png.caption: Among studies that name a funder, 53% name national governments. A study may name more than one funder; these are study counts, not amounts of funding.
fig_funder_types_v5.png.warning: Funder information is recorded for only part of the evidence base. Missing information does not mean a study had no funding.

fig_funder_funders_treemap.png.title: The most frequently named research funders
fig_funder_funders_treemap.png.caption: Larger boxes show funders named by more studies. Studies naming several funders count once for each.
fig_funder_funders_treemap.png.warning: Funder information is recorded for only part of the evidence base. Missing information does not mean a study had no funding.

fig_funder_function_heatmap.png.title: Which financing functions appear in each funder’s studies?
fig_funder_function_heatmap.png.caption: Each row shows the share of that funder’s studies covering each financing function, among studies assigned a function. Shares can exceed 100% because functions overlap.
fig_funder_function_heatmap.png.warning: Funder information is recorded for only part of the evidence base. Missing information does not mean a study had no funding.

fig_funder_outcome_heatmap.png.title: Which outcomes are studied in each funder’s research?
fig_funder_outcome_heatmap.png.caption: Each row shows which outcomes are examined in that funder’s studies. It shows what was studied, rather than what the research found.
fig_funder_outcome_heatmap.png.warning: Funder information is recorded for only part of the evidence base. Missing information does not mean a study had no funding.

fig_funder_trend.png.title: How the funders named in studies have changed over time
fig_funder_trend.png.caption: The lines show each funder’s share of studies naming a funder in that year. They do not measure the amount of money provided.
fig_funder_trend.png.warning: Funder information is recorded for only part of the evidence base. Missing information does not mean a study had no funding.

fig_funder_authorship_alluvial.png.title: How funders, financing functions and author-team locations connect
fig_funder_authorship_alluvial.png.caption: Wider bands represent more studies connecting a funder, one recorded financing function and an author-team location. Only 536 eligible studies are shown.
fig_funder_authorship_alluvial.png.warning: Funder information is recorded for only part of the evidence base. Missing information does not mean a study had no funding.

fig_funder_scorecard.png.title: Gap scorecard: which evidence gaps could funders investigate?
fig_funder_scorecard.png.caption: The chart compares countries’ research shares with their shares of disease burden. The ranking depends on this benchmark and does not establish funding priorities.
fig_funder_scorecard.png.warning: Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.
fig_funder_scorecard.png.basis: Colours show each country’s current World Bank income group (FY2027).

fig_fcas_countries_v5.png.title: Countries affected by fragility or conflict with the most studies
fig_fcas_countries_v5.png.caption: Nigeria and Ethiopia appear in 38% of studies covering settings classified as affected by fragility or conflict. Multi-country studies may appear under several countries.
fig_fcas_countries_v5.png.basis: Studies published in 2026 use the latest World Bank list available.

fig_fcas_trend_v5.png.title: How research in settings affected by fragility or conflict has changed
fig_fcas_trend_v5.png.caption: Research coverage increased. Part of the increase reflects changes in the World Bank country list; the fixed-country comparison also shows growth.
fig_fcas_trend_v5.png.basis: The blue line uses the World Bank list for each publication year.

fig_outcome_by_context_v5.png.title: Which outcomes are studied in settings affected by fragility or conflict?
fig_outcome_by_context_v5.png.caption: Compared with studies about high-income countries, studies in these settings more often examine financial protection and less often examine resource use.

fig_dah_trend.png.title: How international aid for health has changed
fig_dah_trend.png.caption: International health aid fell from its 2021 peak. The 2025 estimate is preliminary; dashed lines show forecasts for 2026–2030.

fig_dah_cuts_source.png.title: Which donors reduced health aid in 2025?
fig_dah_cuts_source.png.caption: The United States accounts for the largest reduction shown, at $9.5 billion. The net decline across all sources is $11.0 billion; 2025 estimates are preliminary.

fig_health_spending_income.png.title: How health spending per person differs by country income group
fig_health_spending_income.png.caption: Average health spending per person is much higher in high-income countries. Dashed lines show forecasts; dollar amounts are expressed in 2023 prices.

fig_aid_vs_evidence_region.png.title: How regional shares of health aid and research compare
fig_aid_vs_evidence_region.png.caption: Sub-Saharan Africa receives 53% of health aid but accounts for 10% of study-country counts. These are different measures and need not have matching shares.

fig_research_vs_spending_country.png.title: How health spending and research coverage are related
fig_research_vs_spending_country.png.caption: Countries spending more on health per person tend to have more studies per person. This association does not show that spending causes more research.

fig_funder_scorecard_combined.png.title: Research coverage compared with disease burden and health spending
fig_funder_scorecard_combined.png.caption: This exploratory comparison combines disease burden, health spending and research coverage. Its rankings depend on how the comparison benchmark is defined.

fig_funder_scorecard_expenditure.png.title: Research coverage compared with health spending
fig_funder_scorecard_expenditure.png.caption: This chart compares research coverage with health spending. A gap against spending is different from a gap against disease burden and does not establish a funding priority.

fig_function_share_quartile.png.title: How financing functions differ between lower- and higher-spending countries
fig_function_share_quartile.png.caption: Benefits decisions take a larger share of financing-function assignments in higher-spending country groups. The four groups are based on health spending, not country income.

fig_outcome_share_quartile.png.title: How outcomes studied differ between lower- and higher-spending countries
fig_outcome_share_quartile.png.caption: Resource-use outcomes take a larger share in higher-spending country groups. These are normalised category shares, rather than percentages of unique studies.

fig_function_share_facets.png.title: How each financing function relates to health spending
fig_function_share_facets.png.caption: Each dot is a country. The small charts show how research shares vary with spending per person; fitted lines show associations, not effects.

fig_function_share_lollipop.png.title: Which financing functions are more common in higher-spending countries?
fig_function_share_lollipop.png.caption: Positive values mean a function is more common in countries spending more per person; negative values mean it is less common. These associations do not establish cause and effect.

fig_functions_vs_dah_index.png.title: How health financing research and international health aid changed over time
fig_functions_vs_dah_index.png.caption: Lines compare changes from the 2010–2011 starting level, set to 100. Similar trends do not show that changes in aid caused changes in research.

fig_revenue_vs_dah.png.title: Research on raising health funds alongside international aid
fig_revenue_vs_dah.png.caption: The chart places research on raising health funds alongside international health aid. The two lines use different vertical scales and do not establish a causal relationship.

fig_function_bump_eras.png.title: How the ranking of financing functions changed between two periods
fig_function_bump_eras.png.caption: Compare the ranking of functions by average annual study count in 2015–2019 and 2022–2025. Rank 1 means the most studies.

fig_function_share_lollipop_no_usa.png.title: Research–spending relationships after excluding US studies
fig_function_share_lollipop_no_usa.png.caption: This repeats the research–spending comparison after removing studies about the United States. Studies are removed by country studied, not author location.

fig_function_share_lollipop_all_vs_no_us.title: Do the research–spending patterns change without US studies?
fig_function_share_lollipop_all_vs_no_us.caption: The two sets of dots compare the full dataset with the dataset excluding studies about the United States. The pattern changes little.

fig_function_share_r_no_usa_dumbbell.png.title: How research–spending relationships change without US studies
fig_function_share_r_no_usa_dumbbell.png.caption: The two sets of dots compare associations before and after removing studies about the United States. They do not measure causal effects.

fig_function_share_no_usa_dumbbell.png.title: How the financing functions studied change without US studies
fig_function_share_no_usa_dumbbell.png.caption: The chart compares shares of financing-function assignments with and without studies about the United States. A study may have several function assignments.

fig_function_share_no_usa_delta.png.title: Which function shares change after excluding US studies?
fig_function_share_no_usa_delta.png.caption: Pooling shows the largest change, a decline of 4.3 percentage points in its share of financing-function assignments.

fig_map_oa_author_v5.png.title: How often studies by authors in each country are free to read
fig_map_oa_author_v5.png.caption: The map shows the share of checked studies that are free to read, for studies with at least one author based in each country.
fig_map_oa_author_v5.png.warning: Access status was checked using DOI identifiers. Studies without a DOI could not be checked.

fig_oa_trend_v5.png.title: How the share of studies free to read has grown
fig_oa_trend_v5.png.caption: Among studies whose access status could be checked, the share free to read rose from 39% in 2010 to 74% in 2025.
fig_oa_trend_v5.png.warning: Access status was checked using DOI identifiers. Studies without a DOI could not be checked.

fig_oa_author_income_v5.png.title: How free access differs by author-team location
fig_oa_author_income_v5.png.caption: Studies with authors based in low- and middle-income countries are more often free to read. “Mixed” teams include authors based in both high-income and lower-income countries.
fig_oa_author_income_v5.png.warning: Access status was checked using DOI identifiers. Studies without a DOI could not be checked.

fig_oa_author_countries_v5.png.title: Free access among studies with authors based in each country
fig_oa_author_countries_v5.png.caption: The chart compares free access among studies with authors based in each of the 25 most active author countries. A study can count in several countries.
fig_oa_author_countries_v5.png.warning: Access status was checked using DOI identifiers. Studies without a DOI could not be checked.
